analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, insurers, and drug middlemen to publish real prices and rebate deals.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved it 25–16 and formally reported it, but the bill never got a vote by the full House before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required hospitals, ambulatory surgery centers, imaging providers, and labs to publish their standard charges, discounted cash prices, and negotiated rates in public files. It would have required health plans to give members real-time out-of-pocket cost estimates and to publish what they pay in-network providers. It also would have forced pharmacy benefit managers to disclose manufacturer rebates and fees to plan sponsors, capped Medicare Part D cost-sharing at the net price after rebates, equalized Medicare payments for hospital-owned off-campus clinics, and set new rules for prior authorization in Medicare Advantage.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, including uninsured people paying cash, who could see prices before getting care; members of employer and individual plans, who could look up their expected out-of-pocket costs; self-insured employers, who would receive detailed reports on drug rebates and net prices; Medicare beneficiaries, through lower cost-sharing limits and prior-authorization protections; and independent physician practices, which would compete with hospital-owned clinics on more equal Medicare payment terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, cash payers, employers, Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals would have to publish standard charges, discounted cash prices, and at least 300 shoppable services in a consumer-friendly format, with compliance reviews at least every 3 years and penalties up to $2 million per year for larger hospitals that fail to comply.

Group health plans would have to offer a real-time self-service tool showing members their estimated cost-sharing, deductible progress, and any prior authorization requirements, and publish quarterly machine-readable files of in-network rates and, monthly, net drug prices after rebates.

Pharmacy benefit managers would be barred from contract gag clauses that block disclosure, and would have to file annual machine-readable reports to plan sponsors covering rebates, fees, wholesale acquisition costs, and net prices per course of treatment.

Medicare Part D cost-sharing would be limited to the net price of a drug after manufacturer rebates, and hospital-owned off-campus outpatient departments would be paid at the lower rate that independent practices receive, with a separate billing identifier and attestation for each site.

Medicare Advantage plans would face new requirements governing use of prior authorization, and the Secretary would have to publish hospital price-transparency compliance and enforcement data on CMS and Hospital Compare websites.

The bill appropriates $10 million for fiscal year 2024 to implement the price transparency amendments and monitor compliance, and requires price information to be accessible to people with limited English proficiency and disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which face compliance costs, civil penalties up to $2 million per year, and lower Medicare payment rates for off-campus outpatient departments; health insurers, which must build cost-estimator tools and publish their negotiated rates; pharmacy benefit managers, which must disclose rebates and fees they now keep largely confidential; and brand-name drug makers, whose rebate and copay-assistance arrangements would become visible to plan sponsors.

drawbacks.text: The maximum hospital penalty is capped at $2 million per year for larger hospitals, a sum that is small relative to major hospital systems' revenue, so the enforcement teeth are modest and the Secretary may waive or reduce penalties for hospitals facing hardship, including rural facilities.

Price transparency by itself does not guarantee lower prices: patients must actually use the published data, and the bill would also largely codify existing hospital and insurer disclosure rules rather than replace them with something new.

Equalizing Medicare payment for off-campus hospital outpatient departments, while it discourages hospitals from buying physician practices to bill at higher rates, could lead some hospitals to close or convert off-campus clinic sites, which may reduce access in some areas.
Insurers and hospitals would bear real compliance and technology costs to publish and maintain machine-readable price data, some portion of which could be passed through to premiums or charges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — letting patients and employers see actual prices and rebate economics before care — is real and the compliance costs are modest relative to hospital and insurer revenues. The bill's weaknesses are its comparatively low penalty caps and the fact that transparency only lowers prices if patients and purchasers use the data. On balance, a good-faith supporter would acknowledge it strengthens existing disclosure rules rather than directly capping or lowering prices.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Ways and Means Committee on a 25–16 vote and was formally reported, but House leaders never scheduled it for a full House vote, and the term ended without the Senate ever taking it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2023, and referred to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Budget.
Two days later, on July 26, 2023, the House Ways and Means Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute (amended) by a vote of 25 to 16.
On September 29, 2023, the bill was formally reported as amended by the Committee on Ways and Means, with a written committee report (H. Rept. 118-231).
After being reported by committee, the bill never received a floor vote in the House, and its action history contains no Senate action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew no cosponsors during its time in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, health insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off because the bill never became law: their standard charges, in-network rates, and rebate arrangements would have had to be published, and hospital-owned off-campus clinics would have been paid less by Medicare. Patients and self-insured employers lost the price information the bill would have required.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows the 25–16 committee vote but not its party breakdown; the sponsor is a Republican, the bill drew no cosponsors, and no recorded floor vote ever took place.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish full standard-charge files, discounted cash prices, and at least 300 shoppable services, face penalties up to $2 million per year, and accept lower Medicare rates for off-campus outpatient departments. Keeping prices hard to compare protects hospital revenue at the direct expense of patients shopping for care.

Plans would have had to provide real-time out-of-pocket cost estimates and publish quarterly machine-readable files of in-network rates and net drug prices, with an attestation of accuracy. Publishing negotiated rates lets consumers and employers comparison shop, which pressures the plans' pricing power.

PBMs would have been barred from gag clauses and required to disclose manufacturer rebates, fees, and net prices per treatment to plan sponsors. Their current opacity about rebate spreads is part of why employer plans and patients overpay for drugs.

Rebate amounts, copay-assistance dollars, and formulary placement rationale would have had to be reported to plan sponsors, exposing how list prices, rebates, and copay cards interact. Manufacturers lose some pricing leverage, though the bill does not directly cap drug prices.

industries.industry: Independent physician practices and outpatient providers
industries.note: Equalizing Medicare payment for hospital off-campus outpatient departments and requiring site-specific identifiers reduces hospitals' financial incentive to buy up physician practices and bill at higher outpatient rates, making independent practices more competitive. Imaging providers and labs face only small disclosure penalties ($300 per day) for publishing cash prices.
